Title: Supreme Court under pressure to take up fired agency head cases

Summary: 
The Trump administration petitioned the Supreme Court to allow the firing of FTC commissioner Rebecca Slaughter after lower courts ordered her reinstatement. Chief Justice John Roberts granted an administrative stay, permitting Slaughter to be fired while the Court considers whether to issue a firm stay and whether to hear the case before it has gone through the lower courts. The Justice Department has highlighted the potential to overturn the 1935 ruling in Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, which held that a President could not fire an FTC commissioner at will. Title: Another Historic Opportunity for the Court: Humphrey's Executor to be Reconsidered

Summary: 
The Supreme Court is set to address the constitutionally questionable precedent of Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935) during its upcoming term. In Trump v. Slaughter, the Court stayed a district‑court order that prevented the removal of an FTC commissioner fired by President Trump, granted certiorari before judgment, and signaled its intent to consider overruling the 1935 case. The Justice Department had already indicated in February its desire to overturn the precedent. The Court’s recent decisions in Free Enterprise Fund v. Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (2010), Seila Law LLC v. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (2020), and Collins v. Yellen (2021) have similarly struck down statutory bars to presidential removal, and Slaughter involves the FTC, the same agency at issue in Humphrey’s Executor. The majority’s grant of certiorari before judgment underscores the urgency of resolving the matter on its merits rather than allowing prolonged uncertainty. Three liberal justices dissented, with Justice Kagan writing, 'The majority may be raring to' overturn Humphrey's Executor, 'as its grant of certiorari before judgment suggests.' The Court will also weigh whether a federal court may prevent a person’s removal from public office through equity or law. The district court’s injunction, which restored the FTC commissioner to office and barred interference with her duties, was described by Judge Neomi Rao as ‘unprecedented’ and a potential judicial overreach. The administration is likely to prevail on both questions, but the Court now has a strong position to eliminate what it calls a blight on constitutional law.

Published date: September 24 2025, 13:32

Title: Supreme Court Grants Stay Enabling Trump to Fire FTC Commissioner Slaughter

Summary: 
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday granted President Donald Trump a stay of a district court order that had barred him from firing FTC Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote, 'The July 17, 2025 order of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, No. 25‑cv‑909, ECF Doc. 52, is stayed.' The 6‑3 decision also granted a writ of certiorari before judgment, meaning the Court will hear the broader question of a president’s authority to remove agency members. Trump and Slaughter are scheduled to appear before the Court in December to argue their positions. The case raises whether the Court should overrule its 1935 decision in Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, which limited FTC commissioner removal to misconduct or neglect of duty. In the dissent, Justice Elena Kagan wrote, 'On top of granting certiorari before judgment in this case, the Court today issues a stay enabling the President to immediately discharge, without any cause, a member of the Federal Trade Commission (FTC).' She noted that the stay allows Trump to remove 'any member he wishes, for any reason or no reason at all.' The Court’s stay is part of a series of rulings this year that have permitted President Trump to remove members from the National Labor Relations Board, the Merit Systems Protection Board, and the Consumer Product Safety Commission.

Title: Geofencing, Geotargeting, and Geo-blocking, in Civil Litigation, Information Governance, and Regulation

Summary: 
The article explains how geofencing, geotargeting and geo‑blocking—technologies that use location data—are increasingly appearing in civil litigation, information‑governance, and regulatory contexts. It begins by noting that most litigation over geofencing has been in criminal cases under the Fourth Amendment, citing the 2025 "Certiorari Petition to U.S. Supreme Court in 4th Circuit Geofence Decision – E‑Discovery LLC (Aug. 5 2025)" and cases such as "Alvarez v. State, 2025 WL 2346165" and "U.S. v. Brown, 2025 WL 1674283" (the court warned that geofence warrants could be "impermissible general warrants" but did not find the 2025 case to support that conclusion).  The article then turns to civil litigation, noting that geofencing is now being used in cases such as "KalshiEX, LLC v. Hendrick, 2025 WL 1073495" (the plaintiff sought to enjoin state agencies from enforcing a cease‑and‑desist letter) and "Pilliod v. Vionsanto Co., 2019 Cal. Super. LEXIS 23599" (the plaintiff alleged that Monsanto used geofencing to target ads to potential jurors, a claim the court dismissed as lacking material difference from traditional signage).  It highlights the broader scholarly literature, citing S. Neff’s 2025 article "Thinking Inside the Box: Geo‑Fencing Technology Litigation and Lessons for the Consumer Financial Services Industry," which argues that companies using geofencing for marketing may face search warrants and that geo‑blocking can influence personal‑jurisdiction determinations.  The piece also discusses practical applications—SpaceX’s 2025 geofence around Crimea to block Ukrainian military use of Starlink, the use of geofencing by employers to track employees, and the use of geofencing by advertisers to target consumers near retail locations.  The article references additional legal scholarship (e.g., "Gavin Small, 20 Duke J. Const. L. & Pub. Pol’y Sidebar 107, 113 (2025)"; "John Ricci, 20 U. Ill. J.L. Tech. & Pol’y, Spring 2022, at 161, 163"; "Steve Calandrillo, et. al., 23 Stan. Tech. L. Rev. 182, 188, 221, 247 (2020)"; "Mark J. Burzych, 40 Franchise L.J. 221 (2020)"; "Bradley Ryba, 20 Marq. Intell. Prop. L. Rev. 33, 39 (2016)"; "William E. Hartsfield, 1 Investig. Employee Conduct § 6:37"; "Lianne Foley, 27 Annals Health L. Advance Directive 62, 62 (2017)"; "Derek E. Bambauer, 58 U.C. Davis L. Rev. 1429, 1435, 1509 (2025)"; "Carson Goos, Elaine McCabe, 26 Geo. J. Gender & L. 245, 260 (2025)"; "Trevor Warren, 63 U. Louisville L. Rev. 187, 187 (2024)"; and "João Marinotti, 100 Ind. L.J. 1931, 1951 (2025)") to support its discussion of legal, regulatory, and commercial implications.  The article concludes that while geofencing, geotargeting and geo‑blocking offer powerful tools for marketing, compliance, and security, they also raise significant privacy, jurisdictional, and regulatory concerns that companies must carefully evaluate.

Citation key: [8]
Title: Liberia: Supreme Court Asked to Review Judge Willie's Bail Rulings in Capitol Arson Case

Summary: 
Six defendants—Christian Kofa, John Nyanti, Eric Susay, Thomas Isaac Etheridge, and Stephen Broh—filed a petition for a writ of certiorari with the Supreme Court of Liberia, challenging Judge Roosevelt Z. Willie’s rulings in Criminal Court 'A' over their bail bond in the December 2024 Capitol Building fire case. The petition alleges that Judge Willie unlawfully kept the defendants in detention after approving their bail bond and accepting human sureties, and that he later accepted new evidence from the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA) after the defense had rested, violating their constitutional right to bail under Article 21 of the 1986 Constitution. The petitioners claim the judge’s refusal to release them and his acceptance of the LRA evidence constitute bias and a gross violation of the defendants’ right to bail, citing the statement that the judge’s life was threatened in connection with the case. They seek to have the bond declared valid, the prosecution’s exceptions set aside, the judge’s rulings reversed, and the defendants released pending trial. The Supreme Court has scheduled a conference on Friday, August 29, 2025, per a citation from Associate Justice Jamesetta H. Wolokolie. The case involves nine charges, including arson, criminal mischief, conspiracy, attempted murder, aggravated assault, illegal possession of firearms, release of destructive forces, reckless endangerment, and theft of property. The petitioners argued, 'The conduct of the Judge in refusing to release the defendants from detention after he had previously approved their Bail Bond... is in gross violation of the Defendants' constitutional rights to bail and the prohibition against imposing excessive bail or inflicting excessive punishment,' referencing Article 21 of the 1986 Constitution. In their petition for a writ of certiorari, filed before Justice Wolokolie, the defendants also cited a Motion for Recusal that was denied. The Supreme Court issued a citation: 'By directive of Her Honor Jamesetta H. Wolokolie, Associate Justice presiding in the Supreme Court of Liberia, you are hereby cited to a conference in chambers on Friday, August 29, 2025, at the hour of 1:00 p.m., Temple of Justice, Monrovia.'

Published date: August 28 2025, 10:48

Title: Supreme Court on Patents Fall 2025

Summary: 
The U.S. Supreme Court's docket for its November and December 2025 conferences includes six pending certiorari petitions related to patent law and Federal Circuit procedure. The leading case is Hikma Pharmaceuticals USA Inc. v. Amarin Pharma, Inc., No. 24-889, which asks whether a generic drug manufacturer can be held liable for induced patent infringement solely by labeling its product a 'generic version' of a brand-name drug or referencing publicly available information about the branded product’s sales—even when its FDA-approved 'skinny label' excludes all patented uses. The petition challenges a Federal Circuit decision that allowed inducement claims to proceed despite Hikma’s FDA-approved label omitting any direct references to Amarin’s patented method of use. This issue arises under the Hatch-Waxman Act, which permits generic manufacturers to obtain approval with 'skinny labels' that exclude patented indications, allowing marketing only for unpatented uses, as codified in 35 U.S.C. § 271(e)(2).

The petition challenges a Federal Circuit decision that allowed inducement claims to proceed despite Hikma’s FDA-approved label omitting any direct references to Amarin’s patented method of use. This issue arises under the Hatch-Waxman Act, which permits generic manufacturers to obtain approval with 'skinny labels' that exclude patented indications, allowing marketing only for unpatented uses, as codified in 35 U.S.C. § 271(e)(2).

articles.title: Big: Supreme Court Grants Cert on Tariff Cases, Expedites Proceedings
articles.summary: The article reports that the U.S. Supreme Court has granted certiorari on the Trump administration’s tariff cases, following a recent ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit that upheld the Court of International Trade’s decision to set aside five of President Trump’s executive orders imposing tariffs. The Court’s order, issued on September 9, 2025, consolidates the cases and schedules oral argument for the first week of November 2025, with a single hour allotted for the hearing. The order also sets a series of filing deadlines: opening briefs by September 19, 2025; amicus briefs by September 23 and October 24, 2025; response briefs by October 20, 2025; and a reply brief by October 30, 2025. The article notes that the Supreme Court also issued an administrative stay on USAID funding cases earlier that week. It includes a disclaimer that the opinions expressed by contributors are their own and a brief editorial note encouraging readers to support RedState’s conservative reporting. The article is factual and does not present a persuasive argument.
